explanation: No single theme: fires on assorted tokens in math/LaTeX expressions (\geq, exponents, fraction braces), code operators (% , mod, freopen), statistical 'range' in parentheses, and scattered function words ('the', 'of', 'there') in prose. Hard to predict; technical/notation contexts are more likely than plain prose.

Mixture: strongest on code-structure tokens such as blank-line breaks after a header/include/closing brace, 'at' lines in stack traces, 'namespace'/'import'/'var' declarations and library names in URLs; also fires on unrelated function words in news prose ('the', 'at', 'to'). Code-file boundaries are the most reliable trigger.

Fires on domain words naming the food and bio/technology sectors, strongest on 'Food'/'food' (especially 'Food and Drug Administration', food industry/services) and moderately on 'Bio'/'bio' prefixes and 'Technological'/'technology'/'Information' in institution names. Unrelated words are near zero.

No clear shared concept: fires on diverse content tokens such as 'paying' (down debt), 'Value' in a variable name, the 'ic' of 'carbonic', 'droplets', 'stream', biological terms ('self-renewal', 'efflux', 'estradiol') and financial terms. Not predictable from the examples.

Fires on the word that completes a conditional or qualifying clause, most strongly 'not' in the GPL boilerplate 'if not, write to/see', and also on tokens such as 'work' in 'those that work', 'commercial license', 'military purposes', 'if by the magistrate,'. License/legal boilerplate is the dominant context; ordinary 'if not' in prose fires moderately.

Mixed: fires on 'binary' in the license phrase 'source and binary forms', '-moz' CSS vendor prefixes, operators in math word problems, 'public' key, and assorted function words or possessives ('of', 'my', 'his') in prose. No single rule covers them.

Mixed technical declarations: C preprocessor '#define'/'#pragma'/include guards, '-exclusive' in 'non-exclusive' license grants, decorators/'@interface' in code, and math-definition words ('finite', 'exists', 'uniformly', \tau); also scattered physics terms ('lensing'). Loosely 'formal definition/declaration' contexts, but several separate jobs.

Unclear: one strong outlier ('Eleven Plus'), then many moderate hits on unrelated tokens such as code identifiers ('ify', 'bindgen', 'null'), math phrases ('integral formula', 'divided by'), word-piece suffixes in chemistry or Turkish words, and common verbs ('put', 'told'). No predictable pattern.

Mixture: digits and operators inside numbers and math equations (years like 2014, '*p', '%'), URL '://' in license headers, CSS class suffixes, and assorted prose words ('to', 'want', 'before', 'week'). No coherent single trigger.

Mostly fires on commas and function words at clause boundaries, strongest in license boilerplate ('binary forms,', 'Permission is hereby granted,', 'Generated by') and Java 'import com', but also on many ordinary prose words ('more', 'the', 'to', 'is', 'or'). Weakly specific; boilerplate text raises it.

Fires on the first token(s) of a document body right after a title line, e.g. the article-opening word in Wikipedia-style 'Title\n\nTitle is a...' ('In the', 'Š', 'P', 'G', 'The'), and the start of a new question or section in math sets. Weaker hits on generic words mid-sentence.

Fires on the first sub-word piece of a word split into several tokens, especially in legal text: 'rem' (remand/remedy/remanded), 'Att' (Attorneys/Attahiru), 'am' (ameliorate), 'Ch', 'Lux', 'COM', '-ap'. Whole common words fire weakly; legal-procedure context boosts it.

Fires on middle sub-word fragments of rare, foreign or proper-noun words split into multiple tokens (Kanan-ask-is, IN-RIA, radio-ul-nar, Cioc-col-aterie, Cyrillic word pieces, polydipsia, Heisenberg), predicting the continuation of the word. Common whole words do not fire.

Strongest on domain suffixes in URLs ('.org' in boost.org, '.com', '.co', lkml.org), plus mid-word or identifier fragments in code, math and non-Latin scripts ('isempty', 'implies', 'ee' of pointee, Greek/Japanese pieces, 'stein'). Ordinary prose words are weak.
